Complete Empirical Research Plan
-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy
   • Main strategy: Within-family (sibling) fixed-effects regression.  
     – The comparison is “internal’’ to the household, so all time-invariant
       parental preferences, wealth, caste, genetics, and village
       characteristics drop out.  
     – Birth order and child sex vary across siblings in the same family; their
       interaction captures the extra penalty (or premium) that later-born
       girls experience when parents have a preference for sons.  
   • Supplement: 2SLS that instruments family size with the sex-composition of
     the first two births (Angrist & Evans, 1998 style) to check whether
     resource-dilution, not just ordinal position, is driving the results.  

   This combination is appropriate because (i) the NFHS supplies multiple
   siblings per household, (ii) child sex is biologically random absent active
   sex selection, and (iii) son-driven “stopping rules’’ generate powerful
   heterogeneity that can be used as an instrument.

2. Treatment and Control
   A. Sibling-FE specification  
      • Treatment variable Tᵢ = BirthOrderᵢ × Girlᵢ  
        – BirthOrderᵢ = 1, 2, 3, … (we will also work with dummies: 2nd-born,
          3rd-plus).  
        – Girlᵢ = 1 if female.  
      • Control observations: (i) boys of any order and (ii) first-born girls
        (the omitted category).  
      • No explicit timing or cutoff; variation is cross-sectional within a
        household.

   B. 2SLS extension  
      • Endogenous regressor: SibSizeᵢ,j  = number of living children in family
        j when child i is measured.  
      • Instrument: SameSex12ⱼ = 1 if the first two births in family j are of
        the same sex (especially both girls).  By construction this is fixed
        before the 3rd child is conceived.  
      • First stage: SibSizeⱼ = π · SameSex12ⱼ + controls + εⱼ.  
      • Second stage: HeightZᵢ = β · ŜibSizeⱼ + γXᵢ + ψⱼ + uᵢ.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
   A1. Within-family unconfoundedness – No unobserved, time-varying factors
       simultaneously determine both a child’s height and her ordinal/sex
       status once we control for age, birth spacing, and survey year.   
       • Plausible because most wealth, caste, land, etc. are time-invariant
         over the short span between siblings.  
   A2. Random assignment of child sex conditional on covariates (for FE) and
       of the sex-composition instrument (for IV).  
       • Plausibility: threatened by prenatal sex-selection; we address it by
         (i) restricting to births ≤1995 or to low-sex-selection states,
         (ii) balancing tests that the instrument is orthogonal to pre-birth
         covariates.  
   A3. Exclusion restriction for IV – Sex-composition affects height only
       through its effect on family size, not through any other channel.  
       • Reasonable because the instrument is based on *earlier* siblings’
         sex, but we will test for direct effects on parental labor supply,
         migration, etc.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
   1. Sex-selective abortion and differential stopping  
      – Limits A2.  Strategy:  
        • Drop births after 2000 and states with SRB <0.92.  
        • Show results are unchanged when sex ratios look normal.  
   2. Age/cohort effects on height (younger children measured at earlier ages
      may appear shorter)  
      – Control flexibly for child age in months and survey × age polynomials.  
      – Run robustness using HAZ standardized by exact age-in-days.  
   3. Selective child survival (we only observe children who survived to the
      survey date; girls may die earlier)  
      – Use inverse-probability weights based on neonatal/infant mortality
        models.  
      – Show robustness with subsample of children aged 0–24 months whose
        survival bias is smaller.

5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data
library(fixest)       # FE and IV regressions
library(modelsummary) # nice tables

# 1. Load data ------------------------------------------------------------
nfhs <- fread("nfhs_children.csv")   # assume one row per child

# 2. Variable construction ------------------------------------------------
nfhs[, girl        := ifelse(sex == "Female", 1, 0)]
# birth_order already provided or construct from birth history
# drop multiple births for main spec
nfhs <- nfhs[plural_birth == 0]

# Height-for-age Z (hazard): assume variable haz already exists
# Key treatment vars
nfhs[, second      := as.integer(birth_order == 2)]
nfhs[, third_plus  := as.integer(birth_order >= 3)]
nfhs[, treat_girl2 := second * girl]
nfhs[, treat_girl3p:= third_plus * girl]

# Controls
nfhs[, age_months_sq := (age_months/10)^2]
nfhs[, mother_age    := mother_age_at_birth]
nfhs[, spacing       := birth_interval_months]

# 3. Main regression (sibling FE) ----------------------------------------
fe_main <- feols(haz ~ second + third_plus + girl +
                 treat_girl2 + treat_girl3p +
                 age_months + age_months_sq + spacing +
                 mother_age + survey_round |
                 hh_id,  # household fixed effects
                 cluster = ~hh_id,
                 data = nfhs)

etable(fe_main)

# 4. 2SLS robustness ------------------------------------------------------
## create IV: both first two children are girls
nfhs[, first2_both_girls := as.integer(first2_same_sex == 1 & first2_girls == 1)]
iv_spec <- feols(haz ~ sibsize | . ~ first2_both_girls,
                 cluster = ~hh_id, data = nfhs)
etable(iv_spec)

# 5. Sample restriction robustness ---------------------------------------
nfhs_early <- nfhs[birth_year <= 1995 & state %in% low_sex_select_states]
fe_early <- update(fe_main, data = nfhs_early)
etable(list(Main = fe_main, Early = fe_early))
```

6. Expected Results
   • Sign: Later-born girls are shorter.  I expect β₂ ≈ –0.20 SD for 2nd-born
     girls and β₃ ≈ –0.30 to –0.35 SD for 3rd-plus girls relative to first-born
     boys, consistent with resource dilution and discriminatory feeding.  
   • For boys, birth-order penalties should be smaller, maybe –0.05 SD.  
   • 2SLS: Each additional sibling reduces a child’s HAZ by ~0.10 SD on
     average; larger for girls.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Sibling-FE design)
   C1: Sex random conditional on covariates ............. 0.5  
   C2: No time-varying within-family confounders ........ 0.8  
   C3: Correct model specification & functional form .... 0.9  
   C4: Measurement of key vars (HAZ, birth order, sex) .. 1.0  
   C5: External validity / representativeness ........... 0.7  

   Average ≈ 0.78 – Overall, the design is credible but hinges on limiting sex
   selection and survival bias.
